title: Talking therapy (CBT) for chronic pain
description: CBT for chronic pain does not aim to remove the pain itself. It teaches ways of coping: pacing activity, changing unhelpful thoughts about pain and reducing fear of it. In one study, after 11 weeks of CBT, the amount of grey matter increased in areas at the front and side of the brain linked to controlling attention and re-thinking pain, and in areas that process body sensations, while it decreased in the supplementary motor area. Brightness stands for the amount of grey matter (grey matter density), not activity. In the first part it shows the difference from people without pain; in "What changed" it shows the change since before treatment.
caveat: All findings come from one small study of 13 people with different types of chronic pain, with no comparison group receiving another treatment; the authors say the changes may come from taking part in the programme rather than from the therapy itself. Pain intensity itself did not improve significantly, although other measures did. Most increases went above the level of people without pain, which the authors read as adaptation rather than a return to normal. Most changed areas were on one side only, as drawn. "Posterior parietal" is drawn on the inferior parietal cortex and "subgenual anterior cingulate/orbitofrontal" on the subgenual cingulate; both are approximations. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before treatment, grey matter did not differ from people without chronic pain in the whole-brain comparison. In a closer look at single areas, only the supplementary motor area had more grey matter than in people without pain.

phases.name: 11 weeks of CBT
phases.caption: Weekly sessions of learning ways to cope with pain. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.authors: Seminowicz DA, Shpaner M, Keaser ML, Krauthamer GM, Mantegna J, Dumas JA, Newhouse PA, et al.
citations.title: Cognitive-behavioral therapy increases prefrontal cortex gray matter in patients with chronic pain.
citations.quote: We used voxel based morphometry (VBM) to compare anatomical MRI scans of 13 patients with mixed chronic pain types before and after an 11-week CBT treatment and to 13 healthy control participants.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: After CBT, there is more grey matter than before in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the left posterior parietal cortex, the left subgenual cingulate, the areas that sense and move the body, and the right hippocampus, and less in the supplementary motor area, which moved closer to people without pain.

citations.authors: Seminowicz DA, Shpaner M, Keaser ML, Krauthamer GM, Mantegna J, Dumas JA, Newhouse PA, et al.
citations.title: Cognitive-behavioral therapy increases prefrontal cortex gray matter in patients with chronic pain.
citations.quote: We used voxel based morphometry (VBM) to compare anatomical MRI scans of 13 patients with mixed chronic pain types before and after an 11-week CBT treatment and to 13 healthy control participants.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: Pain intensity did not improve significantly. People who catastrophised less showed more growth in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, but in the right one and the right hippocampus the relationship went the other way. One small study with no comparison treatment.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: More grey matter after 11 weeks of CBT in one study of 13 people; the abstract describes it as on both sides, and the detailed list names the right side. Less catastrophising about pain went with more growth on the left but with less on the right. Brightness stands for the amount of grey matter (grey matter density), not activity.
